paragraphs.heading: A muscular pump
paragraphs.text: Humans and other animals have a heart, a muscular organ that pumps blood through the blood vessels. Together, the heart and the vessels make up the circulatory system. The blood it pumps brings oxygen and nutrients to the tissues and carries metabolic waste, such as carbon dioxide, to the lungs.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits
paragraphs.text: In humans, the heart lies between the two lungs, in a central section of the chest called the mediastinum. Its largest part is usually shifted slightly to the left. Because of where the heart sits, the left lung is the smaller of the two and has a notch in its border to make room for it. The heart is often compared to a closed fist in size, though that comparison is disputed, and an adult heart weighs 250–350 grams.

paragraphs.heading: Four chambers
paragraphs.text: The human heart has four chambers: two upper atria, which receive blood, and two lower ventricles, which send it out. The right atrium and right ventricle are called the right heart, and the left pair the left heart. The atria open into the ventricles through the atrioventricular valves. In a healthy heart, valves stop blood from flowing backward, so it moves only one way. A fibrous cardiac skeleton gives the heart its structure and forms the rings that act as bases for the four valves.

paragraphs.heading: One trip through
paragraphs.text: Blood that has given up its oxygen flows into the right atrium from the two venae cavae, superior and inferior, and passes into the right ventricle. From there it is pumped to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. It comes back into the left atrium, moves on into the left ventricle, and leaves via the aorta for the rest of the body. In the capillaries it swaps nutrients and other substances with cells, losing oxygen and gaining carbon dioxide, before venules and veins bring it back to the heart.

paragraphs.heading: Setting the beat
paragraphs.text: A group of pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial node sets the heart's rhythm. These cells generate an electric current that makes the heart contract, and the current travels through the atrioventricular node and along the heart's conduction system. At rest, an adult heart beats close to 72 times a minute. The wall of the heart has three layers, the epicardium, myocardium and endocardium, and the whole organ sits inside a protective sac, the pericardium, which holds a little fluid.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Cardiovascular diseases are the most common cause of death worldwide: about 19.8 million people died of them in 2022, roughly 32% of all deaths. Heart attack and stroke caused 85% of those deaths. Among the risk factors are smoking, excess weight, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, too little exercise, and diabetes that is poorly controlled. These diseases often show no symptoms, but they may cause chest pain or shortness of breath. Doctors diagnose them by taking a medical history, listening to the heart with a stethoscope, and using an ECG or an echocardiogram, which uses ultrasound.
